results.note: Both findings are partly met: 'And so, although …' restores 'And therefore', and time is again the agent that brings in successors. But (1) the although-clause is now answered by an invented main clause, 'yet in the end time did its work'. 'In the end' and 'did its work' are not in Locke, and the clause says nothing by itself. (2) Locke's participle ('time, giving authority … to customs, … had brought in successors') makes the hallowing of custom the means by which the successors came. That is now two coordinate acts ('It gave authority … and it brought in successors'), which weakens the causal point the r2 finding raised. 'When that happened' and 'and so they could never be safe' are fine. The rest (senate/parliament, 'legislature', ** mark, anarchy clause) is intact.
results.suggested_fix: And so, although perhaps at first (as will be shown more fully later in this discourse) some one good and excellent man gained pre-eminence over the rest, and such deference was paid to his goodness and virtue, as to a kind of natural authority, that the chief rule, with the arbitration of their differences, passed into his hands by tacit consent, without any other safeguard than the assurance they had of his uprightness and wisdom — yet time, by giving authority and (as some men would persuade us) sacredness to customs that the careless and unforeseeing innocence of the first ages had begun, in the end brought in successors of another kind. When that happened, the people found their properties not secure …

results.note: 'for the whole' removed: 'a right to act and to bind the rest' matches 'act and conclude the rest'.

Both edits are correct: the gloss is removed, 'Caeteris paribus' now stands alone, and 'boldest' replaces 'strongest' for 'stoutest'. However, right next to the edit, Locke's concession 'though' is missing. This was already missing before the edit. Source: 'enjoyed their own natural freedom, though, caeteris paribus, they commonly prefer the heir …; yet if they find him … weak … they pass him by'. With a full stop after 'freedom' and no 'though', the preference for the heir no longer reads as a qualification on their natural freedom.
results.suggested_fix: …enjoyed their own natural freedom — though, caeteris paribus, they commonly prefer the heir of their dead king. Yet if they find him in any way weak or incapable, they pass him over and set up the boldest and bravest man as their ruler.

results.note: Restructuring the main clause fixes the finding: 'are little more than generals of their armies' is again the main predicate, and the 'while' clause is outside the parenthesis. But the edit also silently changes Locke's tense, from 'whilst the inhabitants were too few … gave men no temptation' to 'are … gives'. This is new drift, not in the reviewer's fix. The present tense resolves Locke's ambiguity the other way: it makes the clause a claim about present-day America, where Locke's past tense leans toward 'the first ages'. The reviewer's objection was to settling the ambiguity at all. The rest (moderate sovereignty, council, war devolving command on the king alone) is intact.
results.suggested_fix: So we see that the kings of the Indians in America (which is still a pattern of the first ages in Asia and Europe), while the inhabitants were too few for the country, and the lack of people and money gave men no temptation to enlarge their holdings of land or to fight over wider territory, are little more than generals of their armies.

The invented 'it will seem less strange' is gone. 'But we should consider that …' turns Locke's anacoluthon ('But when we consider, that …') into a grammatical sentence without adding a claim. 'even though' for 'however it be' keeps the concession. The sentence reads cleanly.
Reference is now Locke's form '2 Kings xviii. 7'. Quotation wording is unchanged.
'a point' restores James's indefinite article, so it no longer anticipates 'the special and greatest point'.
'councils' becomes 'counsels' (designs), per the style-note decision. The rest is unchanged.
The gloss 'for a limited term' is removed. 'chosen, pro tempore, by the people' is in Locke's word order.
'and yet sit idle?' removes the 'still sit still' pun and restores 'yet'. Meaning unchanged.

The first 'because' is restored, so Barclay's two parallel reasons now read as reasons, which fixes the r5 finding. But the sentence 'For though perhaps …, yet because …; and also because … into the power and dominion of a foreign nation.' has no main clause: it is a fragment ending in a full stop. The added bridge 'For both these reasons,' in the next sentence makes up for this with words that are not in Locke's English. The meaning is sound, but the grammar is broken. Merging the two sentences needs no bridge. The p43 re-quotation ('because he has betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he ought to have carefully preserved') still matches word for word.
results.suggested_fix: For though perhaps it may not be his intention to harm the people, yet because he has thereby lost the principal part of royal dignity, namely, to be next and immediately under God, supreme in his kingdom, and also because he has betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he ought to have carefully preserved, into the power and dominion of a foreign nation, he himself, by this alienation, as it were, of his kingdom, loses the power he had in it before, without transferring even the least right to those on whom he would have bestowed it.
